strengths: Elegant and technically well-motivated core idea: extending RoPE to a set of discrete reference frames drawn from Platonic solid symmetry groups, yielding combined translation and roto-reflection equivariance while preserving the exact computation graph and cost of a standard Transformer.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides a careful group-theoretic derivation of RoPE (Appendix A), formal equivariance proofs (Appendix C), and a novel and interesting formal connection between linear RoPE-attention and dynamic (group) convolution with linear-time complexity (Prop. 2, Corollary 1).

Broad and diverse empirical validation spanning 2D vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction (QM9, OMol25), testing both 'equivariant' and 'non-equivariant' task regimes.

Practical efficiency story is compelling: parameter count reduction via weight-sharing (e.g., CIFAR-10 84M vs 21M params with better accuracy), competitive inference times versus TFN/G-Hyena, and a promising Fourier-domain implementation (Appendix M) showing further scalability at larger hidden dimensions.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset descriptions, and (per the reproducibility statement) attached source code with plans to open-source.
weaknesses: The claimed equivariance is only to a finite discrete subgroup (12/24/60 elements) rather than full continuous SO(3)/O(3); the paper's repeated framing as 'approximately SE(n)/E(n)-equivariant' is somewhat imprecise and the practical consequences of this approximation (e.g., generalization to arbitrary unseen rotations) are not rigorously quantified.

Some central experimental comparisons are inconclusive or self-undermining: the QM9 comparison to EquiformerV2 shows near-parity rather than a clear win; the OMol25 comparison is only favorable under an artificially matched compute budget, while literature-reported numbers with more compute show a large gap (e.g., force MAE 10.11 vs 24.25), and the 'we leave this for future work' framing understates this limitation.

The key design choice of using constant keys (kj=1) to avoid training instability on QM9/OMol25 is justified only by post-hoc narrative/hypothesis, without a controlled ablation or quantitative evidence (e.g., loss curves) demonstrating the claimed instability of the mixed-kernel formulation.
Appendix B ('Related Works') is essentially an unfinished placeholder (a bare list of method names with no discussion), which is a significant presentation lapse.

The PCA-frame variant (Table 3, '8-Refl + 1 frame') performs far worse than the paper's own end-to-end attention models (0.039 vs 0.010 MAE), yet is used to claim superiority over Frame Averaging baselines (FAFormer); this comparison is somewhat confusing and could be presented more carefully.
Reported wall-clock timings have implausibly large variance (e.g., 2.01 ± 3.74 ms for the standard Transformer), raising questions about the reliability/rigor of the timing methodology.

Guidance on how to select the appropriate Platonic group for a new task/domain is limited; the paper relies on extensive per-task hyperparameter sweeps rather than offering principled selection criteria, which may hinder practical adoption.

The core equivariant machinery (group convolutions, weight-sharing via Schur's lemma decomposition) draws heavily on well-established group-equivariant network theory; the primary novelty is its specific combination with RoPE-attention, which, while useful, is an incremental (though valuable) conceptual step rather than a fundamentally new theoretical framework.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution is elegant and well-motivated: reframing RoPE attention through group representation theory and extending it to full Euclidean equivariance via parallel per-frame attention heads defined by Platonic solid symmetry groups. This preserves the exact computation graph and cost of a standard Transformer, which is a genuinely valuable practical property that distinguishes this work from prior equivariant-attention methods that require costly architectural changes.

The formal connection between softmax-free RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 2, Cor. 1) is a nice theoretical result that yields a practically useful linear-time variant, and the authors provide full proofs in the appendix.

The experimental scope is broad, spanning 2D vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction at both small (QM9) and large scale (OMol25), which helps demonstrate the general applicability of the framework.

Ablations comparing trivial vs. Platonic groups, attention vs. convolutional variants, and invariant vs. equivariant attention scores are informative and support the core claims about the benefit of the geometric inductive bias.
Reproducibility efforts are reasonably strong: detailed hyperparameter tables, an explicit description of the tuning protocol (Appendix H), and code attached as supplementary material.

The exploration of a Fourier-domain implementation (Appendix M) is a thoughtful additional contribution that points to a promising direction for scaling the method further, and the authors are transparent that it is not yet a mature optimization.
weaknesses: On QM9, the paper's own attention-based Platonic Transformer is only on par with (not better than) EquiformerV2 on the reported metric (mu), and its convolutional variant is notably worse than Rapidash (0.012 vs 0.010 on mu, 0.047 vs 0.040 on alpha), yet the framing in the text emphasizes competitiveness without fully acknowledging these gaps. Also, only 2 of the standard 12+ QM9 targets are reported, limiting the strength of the evidence.

The OMol25 comparison uses a highly constrained, non-standard compute budget (120 GPU-hours vs. the 475 GPU-hours estimated for literature eSEN), and the paper's own reproduced eSEN baseline under this budget performs far worse than literature-reported eSEN (e.g., force MAE 23.92 vs. 10.11). This large discrepancy raises questions about whether the reproduced baseline is well-tuned/representative, and the claimed 'outperforms eSEN' result should be interpreted cautiously given this gap to true SOTA is not closed nor clearly contextualized.

The hypothesis about mixed vs. purely geometric kernels causing training instability on QM9/OMol25 (Remark 1 / Section 4.1) is presented as an explanation but is not rigorously ablated or quantitatively substantiated—it reads as post-hoc reasoning rather than a validated empirical finding.

Appendix B ('Related Works') is essentially a bare list of method names under two headings with no discussion, comparison, or citations—this appears unfinished and is a notable presentation gap for a paper otherwise careful about related work in the main text.

The method only achieves equivariance to a discretized/finite subgroup of SO(3)/O(3) (Platonic solid symmetries), not exact continuous rotational equivariance; the paper is reasonably upfront about this design choice, but the practical implications (how much approximation error this introduces for continuous-symmetry tasks) are not empirically quantified.

Selecting the appropriate Platonic group (tetrahedron vs. octahedron vs. cyclic/dihedral, etc.) for a given task requires hyperparameter search rather than a principled default, adding practical overhead not fully discussed as a limitation.

The 'at no additional cost' framing, while largely true for the FLOP/parameter-matched comparisons, relies on a specific head-count matching convention (Appendix H) that is somewhat indirect; broader wall-clock evidence is limited to a small set of QM9 batch timings.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated core idea: defining RoPE-attention relative to a set of reference frames drawn from Platonic solid symmetry groups yields combined translation + discrete roto-reflection equivariance while leaving the attention mechanism, computation graph, and cost of a standard Transformer completely unchanged. This directly resolves the long-standing scalability vs. symmetry-awareness trade-off in a principled way.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides formal proofs (Appendix A-C) that ground RoPE in group representation theory, prove end-to-end equivariance of the architecture, and establish a rigorous equivalence between linear RoPE-attention and a dynamic, content-aware group convolution with linear-time complexity (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.3).

Broad and diverse experimental validation across vision (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and multiple molecular tasks (QM9 regression and generation, OMol25 property/force prediction, ProteinMD), with the method matching or outperforming specialized state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., outperforming eSEN-sm on OMol25 with 2.6x higher throughput, outperforming G-Hyena on ProteinMD).

Thorough ablation studies, including group-size effects, equivariant vs. invariant attention scores, fixed vs. learned key trade-offs with an optimization-sensitivity analysis (Appendix M), equivariance-error measurements before/after training, and a forward-looking exploration of Fourier-domain implementations that show further throughput gains at larger hidden dimensions.

High degree of reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables for every dataset, explicit training protocols, and runtime/timing benchmarks against reference equivariant architectures (G-Hyena, TFN), lending credibility to the practical efficiency claims.
weaknesses: The method only guarantees equivariance to discrete subgroups of O(n) (Platonic solids/polygon symmetries), not full continuous SE(3)/E(3) equivariance; this is acknowledged but somewhat undercuts the generality suggested by framing (e.g., 'approximate E(n) equivariance'), and the practical difference from full continuous equivariance is not deeply quantified beyond one QM9 equivariance-error table.

Some equivariant-task results show only modest improvements (e.g., the validity gap between DiP-{e} and DiP-Tetrahedron on QM9 generation is small), and the paper's own discussion suggests Transformers may already partially learn approximate equivariance without the constraint, which slightly weakens the centrality of the claimed inductive-bias benefit at scale.

The OMol25 comparison relies on a single external baseline (eSEN-sm, 6M params) that is considerably smaller than the proposed 60M-parameter models; a more extensive comparison against other scalable MLIP architectures at matched parameter/compute budgets would strengthen the scalability claims.

Several large-scale results (e.g., OMol25 Table 5) appear to be single runs without reported variance/seeds, unlike the CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN tables, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains.

The Fourier-domain implementation, while promising, is presented as a preliminary/unoptimized proof-of-concept relegated to the appendix and not integrated into the main experimental pipeline, so the practical efficiency benefits of the 'linear-time convolutional variant' and Fourier speedups are only partially demonstrated in the main results.

The paper is notation-heavy and assumes substantial familiarity with group representation theory (irreps, Schur's lemma, Cayley tables), which may limit accessibility to a broader ICML audience despite the otherwise clear high-level narrative.
